title: God has no mouth or voice, and does not change
source_text: Πάλιν τε αὖ ὁ Κέλσος τάχα μὲν παρακούσας τοῦ „τὸ γὰρ στόμα κυρίου ἐλάλησε ταῦτα“ τάχα δὲ καὶ τῶν ἰδιωτῶν προπετευσαμένων περὶ τῆς τῶν τοιούτων διηγήσεως, μὴ νοήσας τε, ἐπὶ τίνων τάσσεται τὰ ὀνόμασι σωματικῶν μελῶν ἐπὶ τῶν δυνάμεων τοῦ θεοῦ λεγόμενα, φησίν· οὐδὲ στόμα αὐτῷ ἐστιν οὐδὲ φωνή. ἀληθῶς γὰρ οὐκ ἔσται τῷ θεῷ φωνὴ, εἴπερ ἐστὶν ἡ φωνὴ ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος ἢ πληγὴ ἀέρος ἢ εἶδος ἀέρος ἢ ὅ τι δήποτε ὁρίζονται εἶναι τὴν φωνὴν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοί· ἀλλ᾿ ἡ λεγομένη φωνὴ θεοῦ ὡς θεοῦ φωνὴ ὁρᾶσθαι λέγεται ὑπὸ τοῦ λαοῦ ἐν τῷ „πᾶς ὁ λαὸς ἑώρα τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ θεοῦ,“ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι λαμβανομένου, ἵνα κατὰ τὴν συνήθειαν ὀνομάσω τῆς γραφῆς, πνευματικῶς. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἄλλο φησὶν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ ὧν ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν· τίνων δ᾿ ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν, οὐ σαφηνίζει. εἰ μὲν γὰρ μελῶν, σύμφαμεν αὐτῷ προσυπακούοντες ὧν ἴσμεν σωματικῶς καὶ κοινότερον ὀνομαζομένων· εἰ δὲ καθόλου ἀκούοιμεν· τοῦ ὧν ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν, πολλῶν ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν ἐξακουομένου· ἔστι γὰρ αὐτῷ ἀρετὴ καὶ μακαριότης καὶ θειότης. εἰ δέ τις ἀκούοι ὑψηλότερον τοῦ ὧν ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν, ἐπεὶ πάντα ἃ ἴσμεν ἐλάττονά ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ· οὐδὲν ἄτοπον καὶ ἡμᾶς παραδέξασθαι ὅτι οὐδέν ἐστι τῷ θεῷ ὧν ἡμεῖς ἴσμεν. κρείττονα γάρ ἐστι πάντων ὧν οἶδεν οὐ μόνη ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ὑπεραναβεβηκότων αὐτὴν τὰ προσόντα τῷ θεῷ. εἰ δ᾿ ἀνεγνώκει τὰς τῶν προφητῶν λέξεις, τοῦ μὲν Δαυῒδ λέγοντος· „σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ,“ τοῦ δὲ Μαλαχίου οἶμαι· „καὶ οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι,“ ἑώρα αν ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἡμῶν φησιν εἶναι μεταβολὴν ἐν τῷ θεῷ οὔτ᾿ ἔργῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐπινοίᾳ. μένων γὰρ „ὁ αὐτὸς“ διοικεῖ τὰ μεταβλητὰ, ὡς πέφυκε, καὶ λόγος αὐτοῦ αἱρεῖ διοικεῖσθαι αὐτά.
pass_a_gloss: Again Celsus, perhaps having misheard (παρακούω) ‘for the mouth (στόμα) of the Lord spoke these things’, and perhaps also the simple (ἰδιῶται) having been rash (προπετεύομαι) about the explanation (διήγησις) of such things, and not understanding to what are assigned (τάσσω) the things said by names of bodily members (μέλη) of the powers (δυνάμεις) of God, says: ‘nor is there a mouth to him nor voice (φωνή)’. Truly there will be no voice to God, if voice is struck air (ἀὴρ πεπληγμένος) or a stroke (πληγή) of air or a form (εἶδος) of air or whatever those clever (δεινοί) about these define (ὁρίζομαι) voice to be; but the so-called voice of God is said as voice of God to be seen by the people in ‘all the people saw the voice of God’, seeing being taken, to name it by the usage (συνήθεια) of Scripture, spiritually (πνευματικῶς). But neither, he says, is there to God anything else of what we know (οἶδα); which things we know he does not make clear (σαφηνίζω). If members, we agree (σύμφημι) with him, understanding in addition (προσυπακούω) ‘of things we know’ named bodily and more commonly; but if we hear ‘of what we know’ universally (καθόλου), ‘of what we know’ being heard as many things: for there is to him virtue (ἀρετή) and blessedness (μακαριότης) and divinity (θειότης). If one hears ‘of what we know’ more loftily (ὑψηλότερον), since all things we know are less than God, nothing absurd for us too to accept that nothing of what we know is to God. For greater than all that not only the nature of man knows but also [that] of those who have surpassed (ὑπεραναβαίνω) it are the things belonging (προσόντα) to God. If he had read the phrases of the prophets, David saying ‘but you are the same (ὁ αὐτός)’, and Malachi, I think, ‘and I have not been altered (ἀλλοιόω)’, he would have seen that none of us says there is change (μεταβολή) in God, neither in deed (ἔργον) nor in thought (ἐπίνοια). For remaining the same he governs (διοικέω) changeable things (μεταβλητά) as they are by nature (πέφυκε), and his Word/reason (λόγος) chooses (αἱρέω) for them to be governed.
pass_b_english: Again Celsus, perhaps having misheard the words: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isaiah 1:20), and perhaps also because simple people have been rash in explaining such things, and not understanding what is meant when the names of bodily members are used of the powers of God, says: “He has neither mouth nor voice.” Indeed God will truly have no voice, if voice is struck air, or a striking of air, or a kind of air, or whatever else those skilled in these matters define voice to be. But what is called the voice of God is said, as the voice of God, to be seen by the people, in the words: “All the people saw the voice of God” (Exodus 20:18), “seeing” being taken, to use the customary language of Scripture, spiritually.

He also says: “Nor has He any other of the things we know.” But he does not make clear which things we know he means. If he means members, we agree with him, understanding “of the things we know” as those named in a bodily and more common way. But if we take “of the things we know” in a general sense, many things that we know are included; for God has virtue and blessedness and divinity. And if someone takes “of the things we know” in a loftier sense, since all things that we know are less than God, there is nothing absurd in our too accepting that God has none of the things we know. For what belongs to God is greater than all that is known, not only by the nature of man, but also by the nature of the beings who have risen above it.

If he had read the words of the prophets, David saying: “But You are the same” (Psalm 102:27), and Malachi, I think: “And I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6), he would have seen that none of us says that there is change in God, either in deed or in thought. For, remaining “the same,” He governs changeable things according to their nature, and His Word chooses that they be governed.

choices.choice: ‘For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things’ is exact in LXX Isaiah 1:20 (also 58:14). LXX Exodus 20:18 reads ‘saw the voice’ without ‘of God’; Origen adds the genitive. Psalm 102:27 is LXX Psalm 101:28. The definitions of voice (‘struck air’, ‘a striking of air’) are Stoic school definitions; left uncited. ‘Simple people’ renders ἰδιῶται, uneducated believers. The last clause (καὶ λόγος αὐτοῦ αἱρεῖ διοικεῖσθαι αὐτά) is difficult: λόγος may be ‘His Word’ or ‘His reason’, and αἱρεῖ may mean ‘chooses’ or, in the idiom ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ, ‘requires’ (‘His reason requires that they be governed’); rendered ‘His Word chooses’, with the alternative noted. ‘According to their nature’ renders ὡς πέφυκε, whose subject could also be God (‘as is His nature’).

'not understanding to what the things said of God's powers under the names of bodily members refer' -> 'not understanding what is meant when the names of bodily members are used of the powers of God' (untangled)
Celsus: 'Nor has He a mouth or a voice' -> 'He has neither mouth nor voice' (οὐδέ … οὐδέ; less archaic)
added 'Indeed' for γάρ, which was dropped
Celsus: 'Nor has He anything else of the things we know' -> 'Nor has He any other of the things we know' (ἄλλο)
'But which things we know he does not make clear' -> 'But he does not make clear which things we know he means' (natural order)
'it is His Word's choice that they be governed' -> 'His Word chooses that they be governed' (closer to αἱρεῖ; alternative kept in note)
checked Isaiah 1:20 (LXX), Exodus 20:18, Psalm 102:27 = LXX 101:28, Malachi 3:6

choices.choice: 6.62, final clause (καὶ λόγος αὐτοῦ αἱρεῖ διοικεῖσθαι αὐτά): the Greek can be read as 'His Word chooses' or 'His reason requires'. It is rendered 'His Word chooses' and the other reading is in the note.
